prompt:
Write 6 short claim log entries (one to three sentences each) by an auto insurance adjuster for a low-speed head-on collision claim, in time order. Injury: wrist fracture. The claimant is represented by a lawyer. Start each entry on a new line with 'Entry 1:', 'Entry 2:' and so on. No names, dates or amounts. (Internal reference C-1259; do not mention it.) Work these facts into the text naturally, in your own words, without listing them:
- The reported injury matches the kind and force of the crash well.
- Treatment followed a usual course and tapered off as the patient improved.
- No earlier injury to the same body area is known.
- Photos confirm some details, but there are no independent witnesses.
- The vehicle damage matches the described impact.
- The claimant told the same account in every conversation.
- The police and witnesses confirm the claimant was in the vehicle.
- No earlier damage to the vehicle is known.
- A neighbor thinks the car was damaged some weeks before the claimed date.
- The driver is named on the policy.
text:
Entry 1: The insured driver reported a low-speed head-on collision, and the policy shows the driver as a named insured on the account. The claimant is represented by counsel, so all further contact will go through the attorney's office.

Entry 2: The police report and people at the scene place the claimant inside the vehicle at the time of impact. No independent eyewitness saw the collision itself, so the account rests on the parties and the physical evidence.

Entry 3: Photographs taken at the scene show damage that matches the described impact, and the repair estimate lines up with those images. No earlier damage to the vehicle is known from our records or the prior claims search.

Entry 4: The claimant has given the same account of events in every conversation so far, including the first recorded statement and later calls with the attorney. A wrist fracture was reported, and the injury fits the kind and force expected from a crash of this type.

Entry 5: A neighbor told our field contact that the car looked damaged some weeks before the claimed loss date. This has not been confirmed by any other source, and I have asked for the neighbor's account in writing to see what they actually observed.

Entry 6: Treatment followed a usual course for this type of fracture and tapered off as the claimant improved. No prior injury to the same body area is known from the medical records requested so far, and the file remains open pending the final treatment summary.
